igcse-0580-ratio-simplifying.description: Write an ordered ratio, use matching units and simplify every term.

sections.title: Why does the order matter?
sections.label: Order
sections.intro: A ratio says how many parts of one thing correspond to parts of another. Read the names in order before assigning the numbers.

blocks.html: Divide both terms by the same common factor. The first term still refers to the first thing named.

figure.caption: Two blue parts and three green parts give the ratio \(2:3\).

blocks.prompt: Simplify \(110:121\). Give the first term of the simplest ratio.
blocks.hint: Use the same divisor for both terms.
blocks.solution:
Divide both terms by their highest common factor, 11.

The numbers stay in their original order to give \(10:11\).

The answer is \(10\).

retry.feedback: That is the second term, not the first. Keep the original order.

blocks.html: Swapping the terms changes what each number describes.

blocks.prompt: Simplify \(182:196\). Give the first term of the simplest ratio.
blocks.hint: Use the same divisor for both terms.
blocks.solution:
Divide both terms by their highest common factor, 14.

The numbers stay in their original order to give \(13:14\).

The answer is \(13\).

retry.feedback: That is the second term, not the first. Keep the original order.

sections.title: What if the units are different?
sections.label: Units
sections.intro: First express both measurements in centimetres, or both in metres. This makes one unit on the left represent the same length as one unit on the right.

blocks.html: Match units before simplifying. One metre is 100 centimetres.

blocks.prompt: A roll is 30 m long and a second roll is 3600 cm long. Write their lengths, in that order, as a simplest ratio. Give its second term.
blocks.hint: Convert to the same unit before dividing by a common factor.
blocks.solution:
Convert the first roll to 3000 cm. Both values now use centimetres.

Divide both parts by 600 to get \(5:6\).

The answer is \(6\).

blocks.html: Changing only the unit name does not change the number of units.

blocks.prompt: A roll is 16 m long and a second roll is 2400 cm long. Write their lengths, in that order, as a simplest ratio. Give its second term.
blocks.hint: Convert to the same unit before dividing by a common factor.
blocks.solution:
Convert the first roll to 1600 cm. Both values now use centimetres.

Divide both parts by 800 to get \(2:3\).

The answer is \(3\).

sections.title: What if there are three quantities?
sections.label: Three
sections.intro: Find a factor that divides all three counts. Draw three rows of part boxes to keep the terms in order.

blocks.html: Apply the same division to every term.

blocks.prompt: Three bins hold 60, 75 and 105 tiles. Give the middle term when their quantities, in that order, are written as a simplest ratio.
blocks.hint: Divide all three terms by the same highest common factor.
blocks.solution:
The three counts have common factor 15.

Divide every count by that factor: \(4:5:7\).

The answer is \(5\).

blocks.html: A factor shared by just two terms is not sufficient.

blocks.prompt: Three bins hold 126, 144 and 180 tiles. Give the middle term when their quantities, in that order, are written as a simplest ratio.
blocks.hint: Divide all three terms by the same highest common factor.
blocks.solution:
The three counts have common factor 18.

Divide every count by that factor: \(7:8:10\).

The answer is \(8\).

examples.title: Simplify a ratio in the original order
examples.question: Write \(20:25\) in its simplest form.
solution: Divide both terms by their highest common factor, 5.
The numbers stay in their original order to give \(4:5\).

examples.title: Simplify a ratio in the original order
examples.question: Write \(56:64\) in its simplest form.
solution: Divide both terms by their highest common factor, 8.
The numbers stay in their original order to give \(7:8\).

examples.question: Two rolls measure 15 m and 1800 cm. Give the ratio of their lengths in simplest form in that order.
solution: Convert the first roll to 1500 cm. Both values now use centimetres.

examples.question: Two rolls measure 10 m and 1500 cm. Give the ratio of their lengths in simplest form in that order.
solution: Convert the first roll to 1000 cm. Both values now use centimetres.

igcse-0580-ratio-sharing.description: Find one part from the total, from one share or from the difference.

sections.title: How can I split a total fairly?
sections.label: Total
sections.intro: Draw one box for each part. The whole amount fills all the boxes. The equal boxes represent equal amounts.

blocks.html: Add the terms. Divide the total by that sum. Multiply by the number of parts in the wanted share.

figure.alt: Two shares represented by five equal boxes
figure.caption: The five equal boxes cover the whole amount. Each has the same value.

blocks.prompt: A workshop shares 165 tiles between Art and Design in the ratio \(4:7\). How many tiles does Design receive?
blocks.hint: Add the ratio terms before dividing the total.
blocks.solution:
There are 11 equal parts. Divide the total, 165, by 11 to find 15 tiles per part.

Design has 7 parts. Multiply 7 by 15.

The answer is \(105\).

retry.feedback: This is the number of tiles for one part. Design has several parts.

blocks.html: The values in the ratio count parts. They are not the amounts being shared.

blocks.prompt: A workshop shares 306 tiles between Art and Design in the ratio \(7:10\). How many tiles does Design receive?
blocks.hint: Add the ratio terms before dividing the total.
blocks.solution:
There are 17 equal parts. Divide the total, 306, by 17 to find 18 tiles per part.

Design has 10 parts. Multiply 10 by 18.

The answer is \(180\).

retry.feedback: This is the number of tiles for one part. Design has several parts.

sections.title: What if one share is known?
sections.label: Known
sections.intro: Circle only the boxes for the person or group whose share is given. Divide that share by the number of boxes you circled.

blocks.html: Use the known person's part count to find the value of one part.

blocks.prompt: Two teams collect cans in the ratio Red to Blue \(5:6\). Red collects 75 cans. How many does Blue collect?
blocks.hint: Here the known amount belongs to one group. Divide by the term for that group.
blocks.solution:
The known 75 cans correspond to 5 parts. That makes 15 cans per part.

Blue gets 6 of those equal parts.

The answer is \(90\).

blocks.html: Adding the two terms would divide by the total part count, which belongs to the whole amount.

blocks.prompt: Two teams collect cans in the ratio Red to Blue \(8:9\). Red collects 144 cans. How many does Blue collect?
blocks.hint: Here the known amount belongs to one group. Divide by the term for that group.
blocks.solution:
The known 144 cans correspond to 8 parts. That makes 18 cans per part.

Blue gets 9 of those equal parts.

The answer is \(162\).

sections.title: What if the difference is given?
sections.label: Difference
sections.intro: Draw the two rows from the same starting point. The extra boxes in the longer row show what the difference is worth.

blocks.html: Subtract the terms to find how many parts the difference represents.

blocks.prompt: Inez and Lee save money in the ratio \(7:11\). Lee has £60 more than Inez. How much do they have together, in pounds?
blocks.hint: The difference belongs to the gap between the shares, so use subtraction first.
blocks.solution:
The difference in shares is \(11-7=4\) parts. Divide £60 by 4 to get £15 for one part.

Together they have 18 parts of £15 each.

The answer is \(270\).

blocks.html: The difference between amounts does not tell you the total share.

blocks.prompt: Inez and Lee save money in the ratio \(4:7\). Lee has £54 more than Inez. How much do they have together, in pounds?
blocks.hint: The difference belongs to the gap between the shares, so use subtraction first.
blocks.solution:
The difference in shares is \(7-4=3\) parts. Divide £54 by 3 to get £18 for one part.

Together they have 11 parts of £18 each.

The answer is \(198\).

igcse-0580-ratio-scale.description: Scale quantities using the unitary method and move between map lengths and real distances.

sections.title: How do I scale an ingredient?
sections.label: Recipe
sections.intro: Divide by the starting number of servings. The amount for one serving is the bridge to any other serving size.

blocks.html: Work down to one, then scale up to the new number of servings.

ServingsRice
4120 g
130 g
7210 g

Work down to one serving before scaling up.

blocks.prompt: A recipe for 7 people uses 490 g of rice. How much rice is needed for 9 people at the same serving size?
blocks.hint: Find the amount per person first.
blocks.solution:
Divide the starting amount by 7 to find 70 g per person.

For 9 people, use 9 of those servings.

The answer is \(630\).

blocks.html: Changing the servings by two does not mean adding two grams.

blocks.prompt: A recipe for 5 people uses 425 g of rice. How much rice is needed for 12 people at the same serving size?
blocks.hint: Find the amount per person first.
blocks.solution:
Divide the starting amount by 5 to find 85 g per person.

For 12 people, use 12 of those servings.

The answer is \(1020\).

sections.title: How do I read a map scale?
sections.label: Ground
sections.intro: One unit on the map represents several of the same units on the ground. First choose centimetres so that the map and real units match.

blocks.html: A scale \(1:40000\) means 1 map centimetre represents 40,000 ground centimetres, or 400 m.

figure.alt: Scale bar with three evenly spaced marks
figure.caption: On the original scale, each one-centimetre step represents 400 metres.

blocks.prompt: On a map with scale \(1:40000\), a paved route is 12 cm long. What is its real length in metres?
blocks.hint: The scale ratio compares matching units. Convert centimetres into metres afterwards.
blocks.solution:
12 map centimetres represent \(12\times 40000\) real centimetres.

Divide 480000 real centimetres by 100 to turn them into metres.

The answer is \(4800\).

retry.feedback: That is the number of centimetres. How many centimetres make one metre?

blocks.html: Convert to the requested unit after applying the scale.

blocks.prompt: On a map with scale \(1:70000\), a paved route is 15 cm long. What is its real length in metres?
blocks.hint: The scale ratio compares matching units. Convert centimetres into metres afterwards.
blocks.solution:
15 map centimetres represent \(15\times 70000\) real centimetres.

Divide 1050000 real centimetres by 100 to turn them into metres.

The answer is \(10500\).

retry.feedback: That is the number of centimetres. How many centimetres make one metre?

sections.title: How do I get back to a length on the map?
sections.label: Reverse
sections.intro: Find the ground distance that corresponds to one map centimetre. Count how many such units the full distance contains.

blocks.html: Divide the real distance by the real length represented by one map centimetre.

blocks.prompt: A pathway is 6500 m long. On a plan drawn at \(1:50000\), how many centimetres long is the pathway?
blocks.hint: Convert the ground distance and the scale to matching units before dividing.
blocks.solution:
One map centimetre represents 50000 cm on the ground, or 500 m.

Find how many of those ground-distance units fit in 6500 m.

The answer is \(13\).

blocks.html: Use matching units in the division. Metres and centimetres cannot be divided as if they were the same unit.

blocks.prompt: A pathway is 12800 m long. On a plan drawn at \(1:80000\), how many centimetres long is the pathway?
blocks.hint: Convert the ground distance and the scale to matching units before dividing.
blocks.solution:
One map centimetre represents 80000 cm on the ground, or 800 m.

Find how many of those ground-distance units fit in 12800 m.

The answer is \(16\).

igcse-0580-ratio-best-value.description: Compare prices using the cost per item or per unit and recognise equal value.

sections.title: What does per item mean?
sections.label: One
sections.intro: A price per item tells you the cost of one equal item. The same idea works per metre, per kilogram or per litre.

blocks.html: Divide price by quantity. Keep track of the price unit and the quantity unit.

blocks.prompt: A bag of 7 seed packets costs 224 p. Find the cost of one seed packet in pence.
blocks.hint: Divide the full cost by the number of items.
blocks.solution:
The total price 224 p buys 7 packets.

Divide 224 by 7.

The answer is \(32\).

blocks.html: Use the full number of items even when the pack contains several groups.

blocks.prompt: A bag of 10 seed packets costs 350 p. Find the cost of one seed packet in pence.
blocks.hint: Divide the full cost by the number of items.
blocks.solution:
The total price 350 p buys 10 packets.

Divide 350 by 10.

The answer is \(35\).

sections.title: Which pack gives better value?
sections.label: Unequal
sections.intro: Compare packs by pricing the same unit. A large pack can be cheaper per unit even if its total price is higher.

blocks.html: Find the price per unit for both packs and choose the lower one.

figure.alt: Two packs of different sizes with the first unit highlighted
figure.caption: Compare the cost of one highlighted item from each pack.

blocks.prompt: Pack A contains 8 metres of cord and costs 296 p. Pack B contains 13 metres and costs 533 p. Which gives better value, or are they equally good value?
blocks.hint: Compare the same amount in both packs.
blocks.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(296\div 8=37\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(533\div 13=41\) p per metre.

Answer: Pack A.

blocks.html: Compare pence with pence and metres with metres.

blocks.prompt: Pack A contains 5 metres of cord and costs 200 p. Pack B contains 16 metres and costs 592 p. Which gives better value, or are they equally good value?
blocks.hint: Compare the same amount in both packs.
blocks.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(200\div 5=40\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(592\div 16=37\) p per metre.

Answer: Pack B.

sections.title: Can two packs offer the same value?
sections.label: Equal
sections.intro: If the quantities and prices grow by the same factor, the unit price stays the same. Checking the two unit prices makes this visible.

blocks.html: Choose equal value when the two unit costs match exactly.

blocks.prompt: Pack A contains 9 metres of cord and costs 342 p. Pack B contains 14 metres and costs 532 p. Which gives better value, or are they equally good value?
blocks.hint: Compare the same amount in both packs.
blocks.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(342\div 9=38\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(532\div 14=38\) p per metre.

Answer: They give the same value.

blocks.html: A higher price for a larger pack does not settle the question on its own.

blocks.prompt: Pack A contains 6 metres of cord and costs 246 p. Pack B contains 17 metres and costs 697 p. Which gives better value, or are they equally good value?
blocks.hint: Compare the same amount in both packs.
blocks.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(246\div 6=41\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(697\div 17=41\) p per metre.

Answer: They give the same value.

examples.question: Pack A contains 8 metres of cord and costs 248 p. Pack B contains 15 metres and costs 525 p. Decide which pack gives better value, or show that they give the same value.
solution: Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.
Pack A costs \(248\div 8=31\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(525\div 15=35\) p per metre.

extraPractice.prompt: A bag of 8 seed packets costs 320 p. Find the cost of one seed packet in pence.
extraPractice.hint: Divide the full cost by the number of items.
extraPractice.solution:
The total price 320 p buys 8 packets.

Divide 320 by 8.

The answer is \(40\).

extraPractice.prompt: Pack A contains 5 metres of cord and costs 230 p. Pack B contains 14 metres and costs 602 p. Which gives better value, or are they equally good value?
extraPractice.hint: Compare the same amount in both packs.
extraPractice.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(230\div 5=46\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(602\div 14=43\) p per metre.

Answer: Pack B.

glossary.definition: An ordered comparison of quantities in equal-sized parts.
Find the value of one part first, then use it to find other amounts.
The ratio of a length on a plan or map to the corresponding real length.
The price of one item or one unit of quantity.

revision.body:
What does per item mean?

Divide price by quantity. Keep track of the price unit and the quantity unit.

Which pack gives better value?

Find the price per unit for both packs and choose the lower one.

Can two packs offer the same value?

Choose equal value when the two unit costs match exactly.
